newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albania reopens airport, moves to secure coast.
newsitem.headline: Albania reopens airport, moves to secure coast.

text.p: Albania reopened its main airport on Thursday and was negotiating for the Italian navy to patrol its waters to stop a mass refugee exodus as Tirana strove to restore order in the chaotic country.

On the political front, rebels who have seized control of the south and are demanding the resignation of President Sali Berisha were preparing to meet to decide their next steps after an ultimatum for him to quit expired.
The rebels have threatened to set up their own presidential council, but it was unclear what practical effect that would have.
In Tirana, the airport which represents the Balkan country's gateway to the outside world was reopened for the first time since its closure a week ago as armed unrest swept the country.
An Albanian Airlines plane with 30 passengers of various nationalities took off for Sofia as security forces patrolled the perimeter and an armoured car guarded the entrance.
A manager of the airline said it planned to resume scheduled flights to Rome and Bologna on Friday and to Istanbul on Saturday. Western airlines are not flying until Sunday at the earliest.
Italian Defence Minister Beniamino Andreatta said after talks with Albanian Foreign Minister Arjan Starova that the two had begun reactivating agreements allowing Italy to patrol in Albanian waters.

More than 10,000 Albanian refugees have arrived in Italy in the past week aboard rusty, ancient ships, many without power, as they fled the anarchy in their country following widespread looting of arms depots and the disintegration of the army.
Albania has also asked Rome to help it re-equip its army and police force, disarmed and demoralised after the unrest.
However the Italian minister said there were no plans for an imminent military intervention in Albania.
"An Italian intervention, much less a unilateral Italian intervention, is not at all foreseeable today, in the coming hours," Andreatta said.
There have been persistent reports in Italian media that Rome plans to send a military force to Albania to secure key ports and the airport so that humanitarian aid can enter.
European Union foreign ministers are due to meet in Brussels on Monday to discuss how they can help Albania restore order and meet food shortages that threaten to become critical.
The head of an EU fact-finding mission to Albania said on Thursday the first priority should be to help restore order and secure safe passage for food aid.

But the report of Dutch diplomat Jan de Marchant et d'Ansembourg seemed to be pointing towards what he termed a "modest (European) police presence" rather than the major international peacekeeping force Tirana has requested, and Europe has already turned down.
"The report is in no way urging the unfolding of a major military presence -- nor does it signal the need for one," Dutch Foreign Minister Hans van Mierlo said in The Hague.

In southern Albania leaders from 13 rebel-held towns, along with some officials from Tirana-based political parties, were due to meet in the town of Tepelene to plot their next move after their ultimatum to Berisha.

The rebels blame Berisha for allowing shady savings schemes which collapsed earlier this year, bankrupting thousands of families especially in the more prosperous south and providing the initial spark for the armed uprising.
One rebel leader proposed on Thursday sending armed men to Tirana to put Berisha under house arrest. However this was met by incredulity and unease from others gathered in Gjirokaster.

Albanian political leaders, now part of the all-party government taking the country up to elections by June, have come out against using force to remove Berisha, saying the democratic process will decide.
"We do not support any military move to overthrow Berisha. We think he can and should be removed by legal, peaceful means," said Social Democrat vice chairman Paskal Milo.
